wine.name: Morgon
wine.classification: One of the ten crus of Beaujolais, above Beaujolais and Beaujolais-Villages
wine.sites: Old Gamay vines around Villié-Morgon, on the granite and schist of the cru, among them parcels on the Côte du Py, farmed without herbicides.
wine.making: Picked late and sorted, the grapes go into vat as whole bunches for a semi carbonic fermentation on their own yeasts, with no sugar added. The wine is raised for some months in old oak and bottled with little or no sulphur, in some years in two versions, with and without it.
wine.glass: Crushed raspberry, black cherry and violet over iron and a cool, stony note; juicy and silky, with light tannin, bright acidity and a pure, clean finish.
wine.ageing: Lovely within a year or two of the vintage, it keeps for five to ten years in a good one; a bottle without sulphur needs a cool cellar.
wine.serve: 13 to 15 degrees Celsius, lightly cool; no need to decant; a Burgundy glass.

label.means: One of the ten crus, around Villié-Morgon; as a cru it need not print the word Beaujolais.
The domaine's name, which his son and daughter kept after his death in 2010.

records.table: Marcel Lapierre's Morgon is the wine of the domaine at the root of natural Beaujolais: old vine Gamay fermented as whole bunches on its own yeasts, with no sugar added and little or no sulphur. Pour it lightly cool for its crushed raspberry and violet.
records.story: Marcel Lapierre (1950 to 2010) took over his family's vines at Villié-Morgon in 1973, when Beaujolais was riding the fashion for Nouveau and most of it was made with cultured yeast, added sugar and plenty of sulphur. Towards the end of that decade he came under the influence of Jules Chauvet (1907 to 1989), a négociant and chemist of the Beaujolais whose work on yeasts and fermentation argued that healthy grapes, carefully handled, needed nothing added. Lapierre took the lesson into his vines and his cellar: he gave up herbicides, picked late and sorted hard, put whole bunches into cooled vats, left the fermentation to the native yeasts, stopped adding sugar and used little or no sulphur. Neighbouring growers in Morgon worked the same way, and abroad the four became known as the Gang of Four, a critic's phrase rather than a society. His Morgon found drinkers far beyond the Beaujolais, and the natural wine movement took it as a model. After his death in 2010 his son and daughter carried the domaine on as he had made it. The movement's argument fits in this one bottle: nothing added, and everything decided in the vineyard.

others.name: Raisins Gaulois
others.note: A young vine red sold as Vin de France, made for drinking soon.

traps: The Gang of Four was a critic's phrase for four Morgon growers, not a body or a label.
Morgon is a cru, so the word Beaujolais need not appear on the label.
Raisins Gaulois is Vin de France from young vines, not the domaine's Morgon.

wine.name: Morgon Côte du Py
wine.classification: One of the ten crus of Beaujolais, above Beaujolais and Beaujolais-Villages
wine.grapes: Gamay alone, from old vines on the hill.
wine.sites: The Côte du Py, the hill at the heart of Morgon: decomposed schist the growers call roche pourrie, rotten rock, rich in iron and manganese, where the domaine's old vines grow.
wine.making: Whole bunches go into vat for a long, cool semi carbonic maceration on their own yeasts, with little or no sulphur; the wine is then raised for some months in old barrels bought from Burgundy domaines before bottling.
wine.glass: Dark cherry, blackberry and violet over wet slate, iron and a hint of kirsch; deeper and more savoury than most Gamay, with fine, firm tannin and a long, stony finish.
wine.ageing: Generous young, it often closes after two or three years, then returns with more depth and keeps for ten years and more, taking on the kirsch and savour of aged Morgon.
wine.serve: 14 to 16 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for half an hour; a Burgundy glass.

label.means: The hill of decomposed schist at the heart of Morgon, printed as a climat after the cru's name.
The cru around Villié-Morgon, with Moulin-à-Vent the one most often kept for years.

records.table: Old vines on Morgon's hill of rotten schist give Jean Foillard's Côte du Py its depth: whole bunches fermented cool with almost no sulphur, then raised in old Burgundy barrels. Darker and firmer than most Gamay, it rewards a decade in the cellar.
records.story: Morgon's growers have an old verb for what their wine does with age: it morgonne, taking on a kirsch and a savour that set it apart from the lighter crus. At the heart of the cru rises the Côte du Py, a hill of decomposed schist rich in iron and manganese whose wines are slow to open, and Morgon became an appellation of its own in 1936. The grower whose name the domaine carries took over his family's vines at Villié-Morgon in 1980, when much of the village sold its wine young for the Nouveau trade. Close to Marcel Lapierre (1950 to 2010) and to the teaching of the chemist Jules Chauvet (1907 to 1989), he gave up herbicides, cultured yeast, added sugar and most of the sulphur, and let whole bunches ferment slowly in the cool. Abroad the four Morgon growers who worked this way became known as the Gang of Four. Foillard's Côte du Py, raised in barrels bought from Burgundy domaines, became the bottle that showed how deep and long lived Gamay made with nothing added could be. Open a ten year old bottle for the guest who says Beaujolais never ages: the hill, not the cellar, is what makes it last.

others.name: Morgon Corcelette
others.note: From sandier granite in the north of the cru, a lighter and more floral Morgon.

others.name: Fleurie
others.note: From the domaine's parcels in the neighbouring cru, perfumed and silky.

traps: Côte du Py is decomposed schist, not the granite of most Beaujolais crus.

wine.name: Côte de Brouilly Les Sept Vignes
wine.classification: One of the ten crus of Beaujolais, above Beaujolais and Beaujolais-Villages
wine.sites: Seven parcels on several faces of Mont Brouilly, the hill of hard blue green stone the growers call pierre bleue, which rises from the granite at the southern end of the crus.
wine.making: Fermented largely as whole bunches in the semi carbonic way of the region, part of the fruit destemmed, then raised for some months in vat and large casks before an early bottling, without the barrel ageing of the estate's Cuvée Zaccharie.
wine.glass: Black cherry, raspberry and violet over crushed stone and a faint smoky note; firm, fine tannin, bright acidity and a saline, slightly bitter finish from the volcanic rock.
wine.ageing: Bright and open within a year or two, it keeps and gains depth for five to eight years in a good vintage.
wine.serve: 13 to 15 degrees Celsius, cool for a red; no need to decant; a Burgundy glass.

label.means: The cru of the slopes of Mont Brouilly itself, a different cru from Brouilly around its foot.
The seven vineyards: the estate's parcels around the hill, blended into this one wine.

records.table: Seven parcels on the slopes of Mont Brouilly go into Château Thivin's Côte de Brouilly, and the hill's blue volcanic stone gives the Gamay a firmer, saltier edge than the granite crus. Pour it cool with charcuterie or roast chicken: black cherry and crushed stone.
records.story: Mont Brouilly stands on its own at the southern end of the crus, a hill of hard blue stone among the granite, and in 1857, as the story goes, the growers built a chapel on its summit to pray for protection from the oidium that was ruining their vines. Twenty years later, in 1877, an ancestor of the Geoffray family bought Château Thivin on the flank of the hill, and his given name lives on in the estate's old vine Cuvée Zaccharie. The family worked vines on several faces of the hill, each ripening at its own pace, and when the Beaujolais crus were drawn the slopes were given an appellation of their own, Côte de Brouilly, in 1938, apart from the larger Brouilly that rings the foot of the hill. Thivin became the house the trade quoted for the smaller cru, and its wines showed what the volcanic stone adds to Gamay: a firmer frame, a saline bite and a few more years of life. Where Brouilly and Côte de Brouilly are confused, Thivin settles it: the hill and the ring around it taste different, and this is the hill.

wine.name: Moulin-à-Vent Clos de Rochegrès
wine.classification: One of the ten crus of Beaujolais, above Beaujolais and Beaujolais-Villages
wine.sites: Clos de Rochegrès, a walled climat of Moulin-à-Vent on pink granite weathered to coarse sand and streaked with manganese, bottled apart from the estate's other climats.
wine.making: Destemmed and fermented in vat as red Burgundy is, the cap of skins worked through a longer maceration, rather than by carbonic maceration; the wine is then raised in oak barrels, some of them new, for most of a year.
wine.glass: Black cherry and plum over violet, liquorice and a stony, peppery note from the granite; dense and structured for Gamay, with firm, fine tannin, turning with age to dried cherry and leather.
wine.ageing: Closed for its first three to five years, it develops for a decade and more, and in time can taste like a red Burgundy.
wine.serve: 14 to 16 degrees Celsius; decant for an hour when young; a Burgundy glass.

label.means: A cru named for the windmill on its hill, not for a village; the word Beaujolais need not appear.
The walled climat within Moulin-à-Vent from which the wine comes, bottled on its own.

records.table: Château des Jacques treats its Moulin-à-Vent Clos de Rochegrès the way Burgundy treats Pinot Noir: destemmed, fermented in vat and raised in barrel, from one walled climat on manganese streaked granite. Dark and firm for Gamay, give it five years at least.
records.story: In 1395 Philip the Bold (1342 to 1404), Duke of Burgundy, ordered Gamay torn out of the Côte d'Or as a disloyal plant, and the grape found its home further south, on the granite hills of the Beaujolais. Moulin-à-Vent takes its name from the old windmill above Romanèche-Thorins, not from any village, and when it became an appellation in 1936 its wines were already among those the region kept for years, firm from the manganese in its granite. Château des Jacques, an estate at Romanèche-Thorins with vines in several climats of the cru, was bought in 1996 by Maison Louis Jadot, the Beaune merchant house founded in 1859. The new owners treated it as they would a domaine of the Côte d'Or: they named and bottled the climats apart, Clos de Rochegrès, Clos du Grand Carquelin, Champ de Cour and others, destemmed the grapes and aged the wines in barrel. Rochegrès showed that one walled vineyard of Gamay could carry its own name and age like Burgundy, and it brought the Burgundian idea of the climat back to the grape Burgundy had once banished. Rochegrès puts Beaujolais back beside Burgundy on a list, where its grape began.

wine.name: Beaujolais Nouveau
wine.sites: Grapes and wine bought from many growers and cooperatives, chiefly on the clay and limestone of the southern Beaujolais, rather than from the house's own vines.
wine.making: Whole bunches go uncrushed into vats filled with carbon dioxide, where the berries begin to ferment inside their skins. After a few days they are pressed and the juice finishes fermenting off the skins; the wine is bottled within weeks and released on the third Thursday of November.
wine.glass: Banana, bubblegum and kirsch over crushed raspberry and red cherry, with a touch of violet; light, juicy and soft, with almost no tannin and bright acidity.
wine.ageing: Made to be drunk in its first months, by the spring after the vintage; it gains nothing in bottle.
wine.serve: 12 to 13 degrees Celsius, cool for a red; no need to decant; a plain red wine glass.

label.means: Wine of the year's harvest, released on the third Thursday of November and made to drink young.
The regional appellation; Nouveau may also be Beaujolais-Villages, but never one of the ten crus.
The négociant house of Romanèche-Thorins that buys, blends and bottles the wine.

records.table: Picked only weeks before and fermented as whole bunches under carbon dioxide, Georges Duboeuf's Beaujolais Nouveau is released on the third Thursday of November. Banana, bubblegum and red cherry, light and juicy, it is a toast to the new harvest, so pour it cool and soon.
records.story: The young wine of the Beaujolais was poured in the bistros of Lyon long before it had a legal name, and in 1951 the authorities allowed the region to sell its new wine before the usual date in December, which made Beaujolais Nouveau an official category. Georges Duboeuf (1933 to 2020), born to a family of growers in the Mâconnais, began by selling his family's white wine to the restaurants of Lyon, delivering it himself, as the story goes, by bicycle. In 1964 he set up his own business at Romanèche-Thorins, buying wine from growers across the region, bottling it under his own name and giving the whole range one recognisable look, with flower labels for the crus. He made Nouveau an event: bottles were trucked, shipped and flown so that the new wine could be poured on the same day in Paris, London, New York and Tokyo, and in 1985 the release was fixed on the third Thursday of November. The fashion carried the name Beaujolais round the world and left the region a reputation for simple wine that its crus have worked for decades to live down. For a sommelier the bottle is a date on the calendar and a lesson in carbonic maceration.
